sections.overview: The tench is a thickset freshwater fish of the carp family that lives in still, weedy waters across most of Europe and western Asia. It is a slow, bottom-dwelling species, tolerant of poor oxygen, and has been introduced to many other regions.
sections.identification: A medium-sized, thickset fish with a large head, a blunt snout, small orange-red eyes and one small barbel at each corner of the mouth. The fins are thick and rounded, the scales very small and covered in heavy mucus. The colour ranges from dark olive to golden. Mature males have larger pelvic fins, whose second ray is thickened. The common length is about 20 cm, and the maximum is about 70 cm and 7.5 kg.
sections.habitat: It prefers still or slow water with a muddy bottom and abundant plants, typically shallow, densely vegetated lakes and backwaters, and avoids fast current. It is native to most of Europe, apart from Ireland, northern Scandinavia and parts of the Balkans, and eastward to western Siberia. Adults tolerate low oxygen and often spend the winter buried in mud.
sections.diet: Adults feed on the bottom, mainly on molluscs, other benthic animals and plant material, together with detritus. Elsewhere they are described as eating aquatic insects and small crustaceans, and the young take smaller prey such as microcrustaceans and midge larvae.
sections.behavior: The tench is nocturnal and finds food more by taste and smell than by sight, which helps it in murky water. It is slow-growing and long-lived, and may reach 20 years or more, although longevity figures in the sources come from introduced populations.
sections.reproduction: Males mature at 2–3 years and females at 3–7 years. Spawning takes place from May to September, in dense vegetation at about 19–20 °C. Females lay sticky eggs in several batches over roughly two months, and the eggs hatch in a few days. The larvae stay attached to plants for several days.
sections.ecology: As a bottom feeder of weedy shallows, the tench eats molluscs and other benthic animals and depends on vegetation for spawning. Introduced outside Europe, for example to Tasmania in 1876, it has become established in places; in Australia’s Murray–Darling Basin it is now declining and rare.
sections.conservation: The tench is Least Concern on the IUCN Red List (assessed in 2022). It is widespread and often introduced, so it is not considered at risk across its range.
